subject: Counting guidelines request: hosted API attribution for system/tool tokens and rounding

Subject: Precise counting for hosted API — system/tool tokens + rounding questions

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — the hosted API looks promising for our product team. Procurement asked me to get a couple of precise clarifications before we finalize the commitment:

1) When a request includes a system prompt (the hidden/system role) and the user prompt, how are tokens attributed on the invoice? Do system tokens get charged to the customer request or to the model (i.e., do we see them in input charges)?

2) We use function/tool calls extensively. If the model triggers a tool that returns a 120-token JSON blob, and that tool response is appended to the conversation, how is that output charged — as output tokens to the model, or as a separate tool payload charge?

3) Rounding behavior: is rounding applied per-call (round up to nearest 1 token/byte or x tokens), per-streamed-chunk, or at the invoice aggregation level? Example: five 0.4-token increments — do those round to 5 tokens or 2 tokens? We need deterministic accounting for our forecasting.

I've attached a short doc with sample sequences (acme-hosted-ratecard-ask.pdf). We're trying to map each line item to our internal cost centers.

Could you confirm the canonical rules so procurement can sign off?

Cheers,
Jordan
Procurement — Acme Corp

Jordan — thanks for the clear examples and the doc. Quick summary answers up front, then I cc'd Ben (pricing) and Karthik (metering) for confirmation and edge cases:

- System prompts: charged as input tokens on the request where they are included. If you set a persistent system for the model on our side (e.g., tenant-level default), those tokens are still counted per-request when included in the context we pass to the model.
- Tool outputs: attributed to the model output bucket. We do not bill a separate "tool payload" line item for hosted API calls — tool/assistant outputs are billed as model output tokens.
- Rounding: we round per-request at the token granularity we report (we do not shard rounding across multiple requests). Streaming does not change rounding rules; final counted tokens equal the canonical tokenized totals for that request and we round that per-request.

That said, there are edge cases around continuous prefix caching and multi-part function calls — Ben/Karthik, can you confirm the examples Jordan attached (I skimmed) and call out any exceptions?

I'll send a consolidated note for procurement once you confirm.

Best,
Kimberly Park

Kim / Karthik — following up with specifics and the concrete examples Jordan included:

Example A (system prompt + user prompt in same request):
- We compute tokenization for the entire input context we send to the model (system + user). All of those tokens are attributed as "input" on the invoice for that request. No special "system" line item.

Example B (tool call where model invokes function, function returns payload that we append and then model emits more tokens):
- The invocation flow is: request -> model request tokens counted -> model emits tool call tokens (these are model output tokens) -> tool returns payload (the payload is not billed as a separate agent charge) -> if the payload is fed back to the model and the model generates further tokens, those further tokens are output and billed as output.
- Practically this looks like: you will see input tokens (initial user/system), output tokens (model-generated text and tool-call tokens our runtime logs as assistant output), and then additional output tokens when the model continues. The tool payload itself is not an additional charge on the hosted API invoice.

Rounding specifics:
- We do per-request rounding to the nearest token (we don't have fractional token billing).
- We do NOT accumulate fractional pieces across separate requests for rounding. So five requests each producing 0.4-token-equivalent (hypothetical) would round individually, not aggregate. In real tokenization these fractional scenarios are rare; the deterministic behavior is per-request integer token totals.

Edge exceptions to flag:
- Persistent prefix caching: if we cache a prefix across requests and do not re-send it to the model (server-side reuse), those cached tokens are not re-counted on subsequent requests. If the cache is invalidated or the prefix is re-inserted into the context we do count them. This is important for your batched telemetry patterns.
- Streamed partial outputs: we publish counted tokens after the request completes; streaming doesn't create multiple billable items per chunk.

If you want, I can draft an invoice mock that shows the line-by-line attribution for one of your sample flows.

—Ben

Jordan,

Thanks for the examples — below is the canonical ruleset you can share with procurement. I've also attached a short mock invoice for the 3 request sequences you sent.

Canonical counting rules (hosted API):
- System prompts: counted as input tokens on the request in which they are included. If you rely on tenant defaults that we inject server-side per-request, those tokens are counted each request.
- Tool/function activity: any tokens generated by the model (including tool invocation markers) are counted as output tokens. The tool's returned payload is not billed as a separate hosted API line item; if that payload is passed back into the model it will be counted as input on that subsequent request.
- Rounding: token totals are integer-valued and rounded at the per-request level. We do not aggregate fractional remnants across requests.
- Caching: server-side prefix caching avoids re-counting cached tokens if they are not re-sent to the model. If your workflow re-inserts the cached data into the context we will count it.

Action items
- Ben will produce a mock invoice showing line-by-line attribution for your sample flows (attached).
- If procurement needs a contractual clause describing rounding or cache semantics we can include a short explanatory paragraph in the SOW.

If that works, I'll cc legal and get a final SOW clause drafted for signature.
